full.preview:
# GLOSSARY — s15 Integrated Harness

Domain terms as used across `README.md`, `ARCHITECTURE.md`, and `code.py`
docstrings/comments. Every definition is grounded in the cited file and
function; entries are in alphabetical order.

### Active request

The running user request that the lead loop tracks as first-class state
(`session_state["active_user_request"]` in `__main__`, passed as
`active_request` through `agent_loop` in `code.py`). Scheduled cron lines
("Run scheduled task: …") are appended to it when jobs fire, and it is what
`compact_history` / `reactive_compact` preserve as the **Authoritative
request** field — the only field allowed to carry instructions after
compaction.

### Agent loop (integrated loop)

The single control loop shared by every lead turn, `agent_loop` in `code.py`:
inject scheduled cron prompts and background notifications, emit a todo
reminder, run the compaction pipeline (`prepare_context`), refresh context and
tool pool, call the model, then either stop (no concrete `tool_use` block —
checked by `has_tool_use`, not `stop_reason` alone) or dispatch the requested
tools and append their results as one user message, repeating.

### Async event loop

`async_event_loop` in `code.py`: the daemon thread ("lead-events") that polls
every second and, when the cron queue has fired, the lead's inbox has team
events, or background work finished, wakes the lead agent by running the same
`agent_loop` inside `traced_lead_turn` with a combined trigger
("cron+team+background").

### Background task

A `bash` call with `run_in_background: true` (`should_run_background`,
`start_background_task` in `code.py`) is moved into a daemon worker thread
(`background-<id>`, own process session); the model immediately receives a
placeholder tool_result, and the real output arrives later as a
`<task_notification>` user message via `collect_background_results` /
`inject_background_notifications` / `build_user_content`.

### Compaction

The layered, cheap-first context-shrinking pipeline in `prepare_context`
(`code.py`)

docstrings/comments. Every definition is grounded in the cited file and
function; entries are in alphabetical order.

### Active request

The running user request that the lead loop tracks as first-class state
(`session_state["active_user_request"]` in `__main__`, passed as
`active_request` through `agent_loop` in `code.py`). Scheduled cron lines
("Run scheduled task: …") are appended to it when jobs fire, and it is what
`compact_history` / `reactive_compact` preserve as the **Authoritative
request** field — the only field allowed to carry instructions after
compaction.

### Agent loop (integrated loop)

The single control loop shared by every lead turn, `agent_loop` in `code.py`:
inject scheduled cron prompts and background notifications, emit a todo
reminder, run the compaction pipeline (`prepare_context`), refresh context and
tool pool, call the model, then either stop (no concrete `tool_use` block —
checked by `has_tool_use`, not `stop_reason` alone) or dispatch the requested
tools and append their results as one user message, repeating.

### Async event loop

`async_event_loop` in `code.py`: the daemon thread ("lead-events") that polls
every second and, when the cron queue has fired, the lead's inbox has team
events, or background work finished, wakes the lead agent by running the same
`agent_loop` inside `traced_lead_turn` with a combined trigger
("cron+team+background").

### Background task

A `bash` call with `run_in_background: true` (`should_run_background`,
`start_background_task` in `code.py`) is moved into a daemon worker thread
(`background-<id>`, own process session); the model immediately receives a
placeholder tool_result, and the real output arrives later as a
`<task_notification>` user message via `collect_background_results` /
`inject_background_notifications` / `build_user_content`.

### Compaction

The layered, cheap-first context-shrinking pipeline in `prepare_context`
(`code.py`)

# The s15 Integrated Harness from Scratch: A Beginner's Tutorial in 25 Terms

If you've ever wondered how an AI coding assistant actually *does* things — runs commands, edits files, schedules work, collaborates with other agents — the answer is a **harness**: the scaffolding wrapped around a language model that turns it from a text predictor into a working agent. This tutorial walks through every term in the s15 Integrated Harness glossary, in an order where each concept builds on the ones before it. No prior knowledge of agent systems is assumed; every piece of jargon is explained the first time it appears.

**Roadmap:** we start with the big picture (Sections 1–3), look at what the model sees each turn (4–8), follow how actions get executed and authorized (9–12), add time and concurrency (13–15), shrink the context when it grows too big (16), recover from errors (17), introduce teamwork (18–22), and finish with observability — how we record and analyze everything that happened (23–25).

---

## 1. Integrated harness

An **integrated harness** is a single, self-contained runtime that bundles *all* the machinery an agent needs: tool execution, permissions, task tracking, teammate agents, Git worktrees, external tool servers (MCP), context management, background and scheduled work, memory, skills, and tracing. The s15 harness is one Python process (`code.py`) where everything shares one control loop, one (traced) model API client, and file-backed state stored under your working directory — no servers, no databases.

That single-process bundle *is* the integrated harness.

# Design Critique: Mechanisms of the s15 Integrated Harness

The s15 harness concentrates an impressive number of agent-runtime mechanisms into one process: a single `agent_loop`, layered compaction, cron scheduling, deny-list permissions, fail-closed threading, plan gates, a locked task board, task-bound worktrees, mocked MCP, one-shot subagents, and a structured trace envelope. The glossary shows a system that is coherent and auditable, but its mechanisms favor determinism over adaptivity: fixed counts, substring matches, hard fail-closed boundaries, and single-field preservation. Below, each mechanism is critiqued with a specific, actionable improvement and an honest weighing of trade-offs, followed by a prioritized summary.

## 1. Single agent_loop control flow

The loop is a strength — one traced path means every lead turn is reproducible in the trace — but it is also a god-function: cron injection, background notification injection, todo reminders, compaction, and dispatch all run inline, and the async event loop re-enters it with a *combined* `cron+team+background` trigger. That combined trigger destroys provenance: a trace shows that *something* woke the lead, not which queue had work, and a failure in one injection path can silently mask the others.

**Improvement:** restructure the loop into explicit named phases — *ingest* (drain cron, inbox, background queues under a lock, recording per-source event IDs), *prepare*, *model*, *dispatch* — and emit a per-turn `trigger_manifest` listing exactly which sources contributed and what was consumed. This is a refactor of ordering, not semantics, so behavioral risk is low; the cost is touching the hottest function in the codebase, which argues for doing it behind the existing `harness_decision` events as a regression guard. Separately, `has_tool_use` is a better stop check than `stop_reason` alone, but it conflates "model chose to stop" with "model emitted a malformed tool block." # TEST PLAN — s15 Integrated Harness Runtime Behaviours

**Basis:** `s15_integrated_harness/GLOSSARY.md` (read once; all expected results below are grounded in its definitions of `agent_loop`, `prepare_context`, `CronJob`, background tasks, `RecoveryState`/`with_retry`, `permission_hook`, plan gates, task board, worktrees, `MCP_HOST_POLICY`, trace envelope, hooks, and related terms).

## 1. Scope & Introduction

This plan verifies the runtime behaviours of the s15 integrated harness: a single Python process (`code.py`) that runs one shared lead control loop (`agent_loop`) over tool dispatch, permissions/hooks, todo & task board, teams, worktrees, MCP, compaction, background execution, cron, memory/skills, and tracing with file-backed state under the working directory. The goal is to confirm that each mechanism behaves as the glossary defines it — including ordering guarantees, thresholds, fail-closed boundaries, durability, and at-least-once delivery — and that every control-flow branch is faithfully recorded in traces.

Out of scope: model response *quality*, prompt wording, and UI cosmetics. Everything below is behavioural and observable.

## 2. Conventions & Preconditions
